what_they_do: Arga Labs builds sandboxed 'digital twin' environments of common SaaS APIs (Stripe, Slack, GitHub, Salesforce, Gmail, Google Calendar, Linear, Notion, and others) so AI agents and their code can be tested against realistic, resettable copies of those services instead of live production systems. Twins are paired with seeded test scenarios and automated CI grading that scores agent runs against defined criteria. This replaces the manual, ad hoc process of testing agents against real accounts or building one-off internal mocks per integration, catching bad state handling, permission errors, or retry loops before they reach customers.
vertical: AI developer tools / agent testing infrastructure
theme_fit_rationale: Arga builds the sandbox-environment layer for agentic software that Theme 3 explicitly calls out (agents as the dominant users of software need rebuilt, machine-readable, testable infrastructure); their SaaS twins let agents safely interact with third-party APIs pre-production.

recent_signals.summary: TechCrunch named Arga Labs one of 11 standout startups from YC's Spring 2026 Demo Day, citing investor interest in solving the agent-testing bottleneck.
Reported growth from $0 to $40K MRR in 7 weeks following YC launch, per a pitch-deck teardown piece.

prior_insights: Phillip, I was reading about the pivot mid-YC from testing AI-generated code to building full sandbox environments for AI agents, and I think it's the right move. The problem gets way harder when agents are making Stripe charges and sending Slack messages in production versus just writing code that a human reviews. Curious how the onboarding experience works for teams that want to add new SaaS twins beyond the ones you already support.

Phillip, circling back on this. I'm curious how the customer conversations are going now that you've broadened from code testing to full agent sandboxes. That's a bigger problem to solve but also harder to scope. Are teams coming to you with a specific agent they need to test, or are they looking for general infrastructure they can build on?

Phillip, one more thought. We've worked with companies across the dev tools and infrastructure space, and Chris on our team has experience with Datadog and companies building developer-facing products. If it would be useful to compare notes on pricing models and enterprise sales motion for infrastructure tools, happy to make an intro.

If now isn't the right time, totally understand.
